L13: A new Federal Trade Commission staff report that examines the data collection and use practices of major social media and video streaming services shows they engaged in vast surveillance of consumers in order to monetize their personal information while failing to adequately protect users online, especially children and teens.
L14: The 【11†staff report】 is based on responses to 【12†6(b) orders】 issued in December 2020 to nine companies including some of the largest social media and video streaming services: Amazon.com, Inc., which owns the gaming platform Twitch; Facebook, Inc. (now Meta Platforms, Inc.); YouTube LLC; Twitter, Inc. (now X Corp.); Snap Inc.; ByteDance Ltd., which owns the video-sharing platform TikTok; Discord Inc.; Reddit, Inc.; and WhatsApp Inc.
L15: The orders asked for information about how the companies collect, track and use personal and demographic information, how they determine which ads and other content are shown to consumers, whether and how they apply algorithms or data analytics to personal and demographic information, and how their practices impact children and teens.
L16: 
L17: Image
L18: 
L19: 【13†Image: Social Media 6B】
L20: “The report lays out how social media and video streaming companies harvest an enormous amount of Americans’ personal data and monetize it to the tune of billions of dollars a year,” said FTC Chair Lina M. Khan. “While lucrative for the companies, these surveillance practices can endanger people’s privacy, threaten their freedoms, and expose them to a host of harms, from identity theft to stalking. Several firms’ failure to adequately protect kids and teens online is especially troubling.
L21: The Report’s findings are timely, particularly as state and federal policymakers consider legislation to protect people from abusive data practices.”
L22: The report found that the companies collected and could indefinitely retain troves of data, including information from data brokers, and about both users and non-users of their platforms. The staff report further highlights that many companies engaged in broad data sharing that raises serious concerns regarding the adequacy of the companies’ data handling controls and oversight.
L23: In particular, the staff report noted that the companies’ data collection, minimization and retention practices were “woefully inadequate.” In addition, the staff report found that some companies did not delete all user data in response to user deletion requests.
L24: The staff report also found that the business models of many of the companies incentivized mass collection of user data to monetize, especially through targeted advertising, which accounts for most of their revenue. It further noted that those incentives were in tension with user privacy, and therefore posed risks to users’ privacy.
L25: Notably, the report found that some companies deployed privacy-invasive tracking technologies, such as pixels, to facilitate advertising to users based on preferences and interests.
L26: Additionally, the staff report highlighted the many ways in which the companies fed users’ and non-users’ personal information into their automated systems, including for use by their algorithms, data analytics, and AI. The report found that users and non-users had little or no way to opt out of how their data was used by these automated systems, and that there were differing, inconsistent, and inadequate approaches to monitoring and testing the use of automated systems.
L27: Furthermore, the staff report concluded that the social media and video streaming services didn’t adequately protect children and teens on their sites. The report cited research that found social media and digital technology contributed to negative mental health impacts on young users.
L28: Based on the data collected, the staff report said many companies assert that there are no children on their platforms because their services were not directed to children or did not allow children to create accounts. The staff report noted that this was an apparent attempt to avoid liability under the 【14†Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act Rule】.
L29: The staff report found that the social media and video streaming services often treated teens the same as adult users, with most companies allowing teens on their platforms with no account restrictions.
L30: The report also noted some of the potential competition implications of the companies’ data practices. It noted that companies that amass significant amounts of user data may be in a position to achieve market dominance, which may lead to harmful practices with companies prioritizing acquiring data at the expense of user privacy. It noted that when there is limited competition among social media and video streaming services, consumers will have limited choices.

L173: # Union Membership (Annual) News Release
L174: 
L175:     For release 10:00 a.m. (ET) Tuesday, January 28, 2025		                       USDL-25-0105
L176: 
L177:     Technical information:  (202) 691-6378  *  cpsinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/cps
L178:     Media contact:          (202) 691-5902  *  PressOffice@bls.gov

L181:                                   UNION MEMBERS -- 2024
L182: 
L183: 
L184:     The union membership rate--the percent of wage and salary workers who were members of
L185:     unions--was 9.9 percent in 2024, little changed from the prior year, the U.S. Bureau
L186:     of Labor Statistics reported today. The number of wage and salary workers belonging
L187:     to unions, at 14.3 million, also showed little movement over the year. In 1983, the
L188:     first year for which comparable data are available, the union membership rate was
L189:     20.1 percent and there were 17.7 million union members.
L190: 
L191:     These data on union membership are collected as part of the Current Population Survey
L192:     (CPS), a monthly sample survey of about 60,000 eligible households that obtains
L193:     information on employment and unemployment among the nation's civilian noninstitutional
L194:     population age 16 and over. For further information, see the Technical Note in this
L195:     news release.
L196: 
L197:     Highlights from the 2024 data:
L198: 
L199:      --The union membership rate of public-sector workers (32.2 percent) continued to be
L200:        more than five times higher than the rate of private-sector workers (5.9 percent).
L201:        (See table 3.)
L202: 
L203:      --The highest unionization rates were among workers in education, training, and
L204:        library occupations (32.3 percent) and protective service occupations (29.6 percent).
L205:        (See table 3.)
L206: 
L207:      --Men continued to have a higher union membership rate (10.2 percent) than women
L208:        (9.5 percent). (See table 1.)
L209: 
L210:      --Black workers remained more likely to be union members than White, Asian, and
L211:        Hispanic workers. (See table 1.)
L212:      --Nonunion workers had median weekly earnings that were 85 percent of earnings for
L213:        workers who were union members ($1,138 versus $1,337). (The comparisons of earnings
L214:        in this news release are on a broad level and do not control for many factors that
L215:        can be important in explaining earnings differences.) (See table 2.)
L216: 
L217:      --Among states, Hawaii and New York had the highest union membership rates (26.5
L218:        percent and 20.6 percent, respectively), while the lowest rates were in North
L219:        Carolina (2.4 percent), South Dakota (2.7 percent), and South Carolina (2.8 percent).
L220:        (See table 5.)
L221: 
L222:     Industry and Occupation of Union Members
L223: 
L224:     In 2024, the number of employees who belonged to unions was similar in the public
L225:     sector (7.0 million) and the private sector (7.2 million). The number of private-sector
L226:     union members declined by 184,000 in 2024, offsetting the increase in 2023. The number
L227:     of public-sector union members changed little in 2024. (See table 3.)
L228: 
L229:     The public-sector union membership rate, at 32.2 percent, also changed little over the
L230:     year. The union membership rate continued to be highest in local government (38.2
L231:     percent), which employs many workers in heavily unionized occupations, such as police
L232:     officers, firefighters, and teachers.
L233:     The union membership rate in the private sector declined by 0.1 percentage point over
L234:     the year to 5.9 percent. Industries with the highest unionization rates in 2024 included
L235:     utilities (18.7 percent), transportation and warehousing (15.8 percent), and educational
L236:     services (13.2 percent). The lowest unionization rates occurred in finance (0.8 percent),
L237:     insurance (1.2 percent), professional and technical services (1.2 percent), agricultural
L238:     and related industries (1.4 percent), and food services and drinking places (1.6 percent).
L239: 
L240:     Among occupational groups, the highest union membership rates in 2024 were in education,
L241:     training, and library occupations (32.3 percent), protective service occupations (29.6
L242:     percent), and construction and extraction occupations (15.4 percent). Membership rates were
L243:     lowest in farming, fishing, and forestry occupations (1.5 percent) and in sales and related
L244:     occupations (2.7 percent).
L245: 
L246:     Selected Characteristics of Union Members
L247: 
L248:     In 2024, the unionization rate for women was unchanged over the year at 9.5 percent, and
L249:     the number of women who were union members changed little at 6.6 million. Meanwhile, the
L250:     unionization rate for men declined by 0.3 percentage point to 10.2 percent, and the number
L251:     of men who were union members declined by 216,000 to 7.6 million. The gap between union
L252:     membership rates for men and women has narrowed considerably since 1983, when rates for
L253:     men and women were 24.7 percent and 14.6 percent, respectively. (See table 1.)
L254: 
L255:     Among the major race and ethnicity groups, Black workers continued to have a higher union
L256:     membership rate in 2024 (11.8 percent) than White workers (9.6 percent), Asian workers
L257:     (8.5 percent), and Hispanic workers (8.5 percent). Over the year, the union membership rate
L258:     was unchanged for Black workers, while it declined for White (-0.2 percentage point) and
L259:     Hispanic (-0.5 percentage point) workers. The rate increased by 0.7 percentage point for
L260:     Asian workers.
L261: 
L262:     By age, workers ages 45 to 54 had the highest union membership rate in 2024, at 12.6 percent.
L263:     Younger workers--those ages 16 to 24--had the lowest union membership rate, at 4.3 percent.
L264: 
L265:     In 2024, the union membership rate continued to be higher for full-time workers (10.7 percent)
L266:     than for part-time workers (5.7 percent). Over the year, the rate for full-time workers
L267:     declined by 0.2 percentage point, while the rate for part-time workers increased by 0.5
L268:     percentage point.
L269: 
L270:     Union Representation
L271: 
L272:     In 2024, 16.0 million wage and salary workers were represented by a union, little changed
L273:     from 2023. The percentage of workers represented by a union was 11.1 percent in 2024, also
L274:     little different than a year earlier. Workers represented by a union include both union
L275:     members (14.3 million) and workers who report no union affiliation but whose jobs are
L276:     covered by a union contract (1.8 million). (See table 1.)
L277: 
L278:     Earnings
L279: 
L280:     Among full-time wage and salary workers, union members had median usual weekly earnings
L281:     of $1,337 in 2024, while nonunion workers had median usual weekly earnings of $1,138.
L282:     In addition to coverage by a collective bargaining agreement, these earnings differences
L283:     reflect a variety of factors, including variations in the distributions of union members
L284:     and nonunion employees by occupation, industry, age, firm size, or geographic region.
L285:     (See tables 2 and 4.)
L286: 
L287:     Union Membership by State
L288: 
L289:     In 2024, 30 states had union membership rates below the U.S. average (9.9 percent),
L290:     while 20 states and the District of Columbia had rates above it. All states in both the
L291:     East South Central and West South Central divisions had union membership rates below the
L292:     national average, while all states in both the Middle Atlantic and Pacific divisions had
L293:     rates above it. (See table 5.)
L294: 
L295:     Ten states had union membership rates below 5.0 percent in 2024. North Carolina had the
L296:     lowest rate (2.4 percent). The next lowest rates were in South Dakota and South Carolina
L297:     (2.7 percent and 2.8 percent, respectively). Two states had union membership rates over
L298:     20.0 percent in 2024: Hawaii (26.5 percent) and New York (20.6 percent).
L299: 
L300:     In 2024, about 29 percent of the 14.3 million union members lived in just two states
L301:     (California at 2.4 million and New York at 1.7 million). However, these two states
L302:     accounted for 17 percent of wage and salary employment nationally.
L303: 
L304: 
L305: 
L306: 
L307: 
L308:     Technical Note
L309:        The estimates in this release are obtained from the Current Population Survey (CPS),
L310:     which provides basic information on the labor force, employment, and unemployment. The
L311:     survey is conducted monthly for the Bureau of Labor Statistics by the U.S. Census Bureau
L312:     from a scientifically selected national sample of about 60,000 eligible households. The
L313:     union membership and earnings data are tabulated from one-quarter of the CPS monthly
L314:     sample and are limited to wage and salary workers. All self-employed workers are
L315:     excluded.
L316: 
L317:        Beginning in January of each year, data reflect revised population controls used in
L318:     the CPS. Additional information about population controls is available on the BLS
L319:     website at www.bls.gov/cps/documentation.htm#pop.
L320:

L57: The FBI’s crime statistics estimates, based on reported data, show a violent crime occurred, on average, every 25.9 seconds in 2024. The breakdown shows on average a murder occurred every 31.1 minutes and a rape occurred every 4.1 minutes. National violent crime decreased an estimated 4.5% in 2024 compared to 2023 estimates:
L58:   * Murder and non-negligent manslaughter recorded a 2024 estimated nationwide decrease of 14.9% compared to the previous year.
L59:   * In 2024, the estimated number of offenses in the revised rape category saw an estimated 5.2% decrease.
L60:   * Aggravated assault figures decreased an estimated 3.0% in 2024.
L61:   * Robbery showed an estimated decrease of 8.9% nationally.
L62: In 2024, 16,419 agencies participated in the Hate Crime collection, population coverage of 95.1% of the U.S. population. Law enforcement agencies submitted incident reports involving 11,679 criminal incidents and 13,683 related offenses as being motivated by bias toward race, ethnicity, ancestry, religion, sexual orientation, disability, gender, and gender identity.
L63: To publish a national trend, the FBI’s UCR Program used a dataset of reported hate crime incidents and reported zero incidents submitted by participating agencies reporting six or more common months of hate crime data to the FBI’s UCR Program for both 2023 and 2024. According to this dataset, reported hate crime incidents decreased 1.5 percent from 11,041 in 2023 to 10,873 in 2024.
L64: “Reported Crimes in the Nation” comprises five parts—“Crime in the United States, 2024,” “NIBRS, 2024,” “Hate Crime Statistics, 2024,” Law Enforcement Officers Killed and Assaulted 2024 assault tables, and “UCR Summary of Reported Crimes in the Nation, 2024.” The compilation’s name has been changed to best reflect the UCR Program’s products, which are based on data reported by participating law enforcement agencies to the FBI.
L65: The violent crime estimate published as part of “Crime in the United States” comprises murder, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault offenses. For the first time, the 2013 through 2024 violent crime estimates are based on the rape offenses reported using the 2013 revised rape definition. The violent crime figures will still be based on the legacy rape definition for years 2005 to 2012.
L66: The revised rape definition (【20†https://le.fbi.gov/cjis-division/cjis-link/ucr-program-changes-definition-of-rape†le.fbi.gov】) encompasses additional circumstances beyond the parameters of the legacy definition. In 2016, the FBI Director approved the recommendation to discontinue the reporting of rape data using the UCR legacy definition beginning in 2017. Since 2017, table one of the “Crime in the United States” was the only table using the legacy definition to publish the historic trend.
L67: This year’s change streamlines the publication of reported rape.
L68: The complete analysis is located on the FBI’s 【21†Crime Data Explorer†cde.ucr.cjis.gov】.

L22: # U.S. Overdose Deaths Decrease Almost 27% in 2024
L23: ## Release
L24: 
L25: For immediate release: May 14, 2025
L26: 
L27: National Center for Health Statistics Public Affairs
L28: 
L29: (301) 458-4800
L30: 
L31: paoquery@cdc.gov
L32: 
L33: Provisional data from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics indicate there were an estimated 80,391 drug overdose deaths in the United States during 2024—a decrease of 26.9% from the 110,037 deaths estimated in 2023.
L34: 
L35: Annual drug overdose deaths are projected to reach their lowest level since 2019.
L36: Almost all states across the nation saw decreases; Louisiana, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wisconsin and Washington, D.C., experienced declines of 35% or more. In contrast, South Dakota and Nevada had slight increases compared to the same period in 2023.
L37: 
L38: The new data show overdose deaths involving opioids decreased from an estimated 83,140 in 2023 to 54,743 in 2024. Overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants (like methamphetamine) decreased as well.
L39: *Deaths may involve multiple drugs, while others might not specify any specific drug. As a result, the sum of deaths attributed to specific drugs may not equal the total number of drug overdose deaths.
L40: 
L41: The data will be featured in an 【4†interactive web data visualization that will be updated Wednesday, May 14】. The 2024 data presented in this visualization are provisional—they are incomplete and subject to change as more 2024 data are submitted to the National Vital Statistics System.
L42: The visualization includes:
L43:   * Reported and predicted (estimated) provisional counts of deaths due to drug overdose occurring nationally and in each jurisdiction.
L44:   * U.S. map of the percentage changes in provisional drug overdose deaths for the 12-month period ending in December 2024 compared with the 12-month period ending in December 2023, by jurisdiction.
L45:   * Reported and predicted provisional counts of drug overdose deaths involving specific drugs or drug classes occurring nationally and in selected jurisdictions.
L46:   * The latest update now includes provisional drug overdose death statistics for Puerto Rico; however, these figures are not reflected in the overall U.S. total.
L47: NCHS releases both reported and predicted provisional drug overdose death counts each month. They represent the numbers of these deaths due to drug overdose occurring in the 12-month periods ending in the month indicated. Deaths are reported by the jurisdiction in which the death occurred.
